data.title: Middle East Eye: Iran defends two-day proposal for peace talks after US rejects conditions
data.author: Alex MacDonald
data.summary:
Iran defends two-day proposal for peace talks after US rejects conditions
Iran defended a proposal on Monday to restart peace talks in as few as two days as the most reasonable offer on the table, after US Secretary of State Marco Rubio called some of Iran's conditions "outrageous and ridiculous".
"Is it unreasonable that Iran demands that US illegal sanctions and its naval blockade must be lifted before negotiations start and that the war should end on all fronts?" Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei told a weekly press conference in response to Rubio's remarks.
Iran has made the offer to shorten the time to restart talks from an earlier seven-day proposal, which calls for Washington to first meet conditions including halting hostilities, lifting a blockade and waiving sanctions.
Baghaei also said US pressure on Iraq to close most of its borders with Iran should not affect bilateral ties with Baghdad, after Iraq's foreign minister said Washington was pushing for such a move. Baghaei dismissed a US military task force aimed at restricting Iran's land trade as a diversion following President Donald Trump's Republicans' losses in midterm elections.
Reporting by Reuters

data.title: Middle East Eye: Eminent Ottoman historian Engin Deniz Akarli dies aged 81
data.author: MEE staff
data.summary:
Eminent Ottoman historian Engin Deniz Akarli dies aged 81
Submitted by
MEE staff
on
Mon, 11/09/2026 - 10:33
Professor emeritus at Brown University, Akarli was known for his contributions to the legal, economic and political history of the Ottoman Empire
Professor Engin Deniz Akarli taught classes on world economic history and Middle Eastern and Ottoman history (X/Bisav)
Off
One of the world’s leading scholars of Ottoman history, Engin Deniz Akarli, died in his home in Istanbul on Sunday, aged 81.
Professor Akarli’s research focused on the legal, political and economic history of the late Ottoman Empire, as well as the Middle East. His scholarship engaged deeply with neglected areas of research in these fields.
One of his most influential works, The Long Peace: Ottoman Lebanon, 1861-1920 (University of California Press, 1993) challenged Eurocentric narratives on state-building and governance that centre western intervention through a close study of the Mount Lebanon Mutassarifiya (governorate) following the civil war of 1860.
He demonstrated that Lebanese self-rule, institutions and local religious reconciliation in this period laid the foundations for secular democracy that was hampered by European intervention.
Born in the northwestern Turkish city of Eskisehir, Professor Akarli completed his primary and secondary education at Eskisehir Maarif College, and graduated from the Department of Business Administration and Economics at the prestigious Robert College (now Bogazici University), in 1968.
He continued his education in the United States, first at Wisconsin University for his Master’s studies, and then at Princeton for his PhD.
His teaching career spanned several universities multiple continents. After completing his doctoral studies, he returned to Turkey as one of the founding professors of the history department at Bogazici University.

data.author: Elis Gjevori

Israel’s genocide in Gaza and the war on Iran have driven a sharp shift in British public opinion
Pro-Palestinian supporters hold placards and wave flags in central London, on 11 October 2025 (Henry Nicholls/AFP)
Off
Nearly four in five Britons see Israel as a serious threat to world peace, according to a survey published last week by the National Centre for Social Research (NatCen).
The figure rose from 48 percent in 2005 to 78 percent this spring, two-and-a-half years into the genocide in Gaza and just after Israel and the US had attacked Iran.
In July, a YouGov opinion poll commissioned by the Council for British-Arab Understanding found that only 17 percent of the British population believes that Israel is not committing genocide in Gaza.
The war on Iran has hit the UK economy, leaving households paying more for energy, food and mortgages. The rising bills have brought the cost of Israel’s wars in the Middle East home to British households.
Last week, the Bank of England raised its base rate from 3.75 percent to 4 percent, its first increase in more than three years. The rise pushes up payments for borrowers on mortgages and adds to the cost of taking out or renewing a home loan.
Before the war with Iran started, economists had expected rates to fall.
British attitudes towards Israel have shifted sharply over the past three years. By autumn 2024, a year into Israel’s genocide in Gaza, 73 percent of Britons saw Israel as a serious threat to world peace.
Israel has killed at least 74,643 Palestinians in Gaza, including more than 22,000 children, and wounded 175,962. Around 10,000 more are missing and most are presumed dead under the rubble.

data.title: Middle East Eye: More than 200,000 join Amsterdam march against Gaza genocide
data.author: MEE staff
data.summary:
More than 200,000 join Amsterdam march against Gaza genocide
Submitted by
MEE staff
on
Mon, 11/09/2026 - 14:35
Protesters want the Netherlands to halt arms sales to Israel, tighten sanctions and recognise the Gaza genocide
Demonstrators take part in a "Red Line" protest demanding "government action to stop the genocide in Gaza" in Amsterdam on October 5, 2025. (Koen van Weel/ANP/AFP)
Off
Tens of thousands of people marched through Amsterdam on Sunday, demanding that the Dutch government end arms sales to Israel and impose tougher trade sanctions over its genocide in Gaza.
Many wore red for the Red Line protest, which drew more than 200,000 people, according to Amnesty International’s Dutch branch, one of the organisers.
Campaigners called on the Netherlands to formally recognise Israel’s actions in Gaza as genocide and denounced Israeli apartheid in the occupied West Bank.
Crowds chanted “Free, free Palestine!”.
“What is happening there is inhumane,” marcher Mike van Dongen told The Associated Press. “As far as I’m concerned, they are doing nothing,” he said. “They don’t dare take any serious steps.”

Large numbers of paid advertisements warned of a Qatar-backed Islamic takeover of Britain in run-up to 2024 election and riots
Far-right rioters hurl projectiles at police in Bristol, UK, on 3 August 2024 (Justin Tallis/AFP)
Off
A new investigation has traced a major anti-Muslim propaganda campaign targeting Britain back to Israel.
The campaign, uncovered by academics Marc Owen Jones and Sohan Dsouza, was at its height before the UK's 2024 general election and the anti-Muslim riots that raged across the country later that year.
It involved large numbers of paid advertisements warning of an Islamic takeover of Britain masterminded by Qatar.
"Between 2024 and 2026, our investigation recorded more than 154m exposures to its British-targeted material," Jones and Dsouza wrote in an article published by The Nerve.
"Its first wave of British advertising ran in the months before the 2024 general election. The ads were also hammering the UK in the winter and spring leading up to the anti-Muslim riots that followed the Southport murders."
In July 2024, violent disorder raged in cities and towns across Britain, targeting Muslims and ethnic minorities, after the murder of three young girls in Southport by Axel Rudakubana.
